name: Pramlintide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved in 2005 after randomized, placebo-controlled trials in more than 4,000 insulin-treated people with diabetes of either type.
summary: Pramlintide (Symlin) is an FDA-approved copy of the hormone amylin, injected at meals alongside insulin in both types of diabetes.
keyTakeaway: Pramlintide is a lab-made version of amylin, a hormone the pancreas normally releases with insulin at meals. The FDA approved it in 2005 as Symlin for adults with either type of diabetes who already inject mealtime insulin yet remain above their glucose goals. Injected before meals, it slows stomach emptying, lowers glucagon and increases fullness; in year-long trials HbA1c fell by roughly 0.6 to 0.7 points from baseline and weight dipped slightly. It carries a boxed warning for severe low blood sugar. FDA records now list Symlin vials as discontinued and the pens with a marketing end date of January 2027.

blocks.text: Pramlintide is a 37-amino-acid synthetic peptide modeled on human amylin, a hormone made by the same beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin. It differs from human amylin at three positions, numbers 25, 28 and 29, where the amino acid proline has been swapped in [1].
Its brand name is Symlin, supplied in the US as the SymlinPen by AstraZeneca, and the FDA classed it as a new molecular entity when it was approved [1][2].

In a healthy person, amylin and insulin are released together when food arrives, and both rise and fall on the same schedule. People with type 1 diabetes make almost none of either, and people with type 2 diabetes make less of both in response to meals [1]. Insulin injections replace one hormone but not the other.

Amylin works on several fronts to keep glucose from spiking after a meal. It slows gastric emptying (the pace at which the stomach passes food on to the intestine) without reducing how much is ultimately absorbed. It suppresses glucagon, a hormone that would otherwise tell the liver to release more glucose. It also signals appetite centers in the brain, so people feel satisfied sooner and tend to eat less [1]. Pramlintide reproduces these effects in human studies [1].
It is short-lived. In healthy people its half-life is about 48 minutes, which is why it is injected before each major meal rather than once a day [1].
Yes. The FDA approved Symlin on March 16, 2005, as a new molecular entity [2]. The most recent labeling supplement on file dates from December 2019 [2].

FDA's own databases show the product leaving the US market. Drugs@FDA lists all three Symlin products under the original application as discontinued [2], and the two SymlinPen listings in FDA's National Drug Code directory carry a marketing end date of January 31, 2027 [3]. The approval itself has not been withdrawn for safety reasons in any record we found.

Listed marketing end date for SymlinPen in FDA's product directory [3]

blocks.text: Pramlintide is meant to be used together with mealtime insulin, in either type of diabetes, when well-managed insulin therapy has still not brought glucose to target [1]. It is not a replacement for insulin, and it is not mixed in the same syringe, because combining them alters how both are absorbed [1]. The label limits it to people who can follow careful glucose monitoring and insulin adjustment under a clinician experienced with insulin, supported by diabetes educators [1].

Across its controlled trials, 2,333 people with type 1 diabetes and 1,852 with type 2 diabetes received it [1]. In a 52-week type 1 trial of 480 patients, pramlintide lowered HbA1c (average blood glucose over about three months) by 0.67 points from baseline by week 13, without weight gain or an overall rise in severe hypoglycemia [4]. In a 52-week type 2 trial of 656 insulin-treated patients, the highest regimen tested cut HbA1c by 0.68 points at 26 weeks and 0.62 at 52 weeks, more than placebo, and also improved weight [5].

blocks.text: The most serious risk is severe hypoglycemia, low blood sugar that needs another person's help to treat, which is the subject of the drug's boxed warning. The risk is highest in type 1 diabetes, and when it happens it appears within three hours of an injection [1]. The label ties safe use to choosing patients carefully, teaching them well and lowering mealtime insulin when pramlintide is started [1].

Nausea is the most common side effect. In pooled type 1 trials it affected 48 percent of people on pramlintide against 17 percent on placebo, and loss of appetite affected 17 percent against 2 percent [1]. Vomiting and headache were also more common than on placebo. Because it slows stomach emptying, it can delay the absorption of pills taken at the same time [1].
